evals.prompt: I run DevSummit Ruhr, a 300-person community-organized backend engineering conference. Our six sponsors each pay $4,000 for a booth, and nothing about meetings is in our sponsor packages today. A matchmaking platform sales rep showed me their numbers - a 38-40% meeting acceptance rate platform-wide, and one of their partners gets a 1.5% no-show rate against an industry average of 20-30% - and I'm thinking of adding a 1:1 meeting program next edition so sponsors get more value. How should I set it up?
evals.expected_output: A reasoned recommendation not to run a structured meeting program for this event, rejecting the vendor's published figures as planning inputs, naming the condition that would change the answer, and proposing nothing that hands sponsors attendee data.
expectations: Recommends not running a structured 1:1 meeting program for this event
Grounds the refusal in the stated facts: no sponsor package names a meeting number and there is one audience, not two separately invited populations
Rejects the vendor's 38-40% acceptance and 1.5% / 20-30% no-show figures as planning inputs, identifying them as the vendor's own marketing numbers
Does not quote any fill rate or no-show percentage as a planning figure of its own
Does not state a meeting length or slot count
Presents running no meeting program as a legitimate, often-correct outcome rather than a deferral or something to fix later
Notes the hallway track and expo floor already cover sponsor-attendee contact at this kind of event
States the condition that would change the answer: a signed package naming a meeting number, or two populations deliberately invited to meet each other
Does not propose giving sponsors attendee names or a list to book against
Warns that only numbers measured on this organizer's own program may be used to plan it
Does not recommend adopting the matchmaking platform, or any platform, as the next step
If sponsor-attendee introductions are addressed at all, they are framed as ad-hoc brokered introductions with attendee consent, not a published program

evals.prompt: We already have registration data for our 800-attendee fintech developer conference, TapStack Conf - job title, company, and tech interests, collected when people bought tickets. Three sponsors asked for meetings with attendees, so my plan is to turn the registration data into a searchable attendee directory that sponsors can browse and send meeting requests through. Attendees can always decline the requests. What should the directory show and how do I structure the request flow?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build the directory from registration data, a fresh opt-in design with complete consent wording, and a request flow where a pairing only exists once both sides accepted.
expectations: Refuses to build the directory from registration data, because consent scope was fixed by the wording attendees saw at ticket purchase
States that the ability to decline requests does not repair the consent problem
Requires a fresh, explicit opt-in collection before any attendee appears anywhere
Asks for or refers to the exact wording attendees saw at registration, not what the organizer intended
Identifies retrofitting consent after collection as the error that cannot be undone
Rejects the one-sided mechanic in which only the requesting side chose to participate
Notes that at community events sponsors get aggregate demographics, never attendee names
The proposed consent wording states which fields are shared and who sees them
The proposed consent wording states what triggers the sharing: the person's own request, a mutual acceptance, or an organizer's judgment
The proposed consent wording states how to withdraw and what happens to already-accepted pairings
The proposed consent wording states when the data pool is deleted
Any directory is published only to the people listed in it, not to the public web
A pairing requires acceptance from both sides, not merely an unanswered request

evals.prompt: Kelvin Data, the biggest prospect sponsor for OrbitConf - our 1,200-person infrastructure conference, second edition - will sign a $25,000 package if we print '20 guaranteed meetings with senior platform engineers' in the prospectus. Our sales lead wants the line added as-is because it closes the deal. We do run an opt-in meeting program where attendees fill in a profile with their role in their own words and what they are currently evaluating. What do I put in the prospectus and in the contract?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the bare prospectus line, a commitment shaped as a guaranteed count with verifiable criteria and a funded make-good (or a best-efforts target), the criteria worksheet applied, and clause drafting routed to the sponsor-agreement work.
expectations: Refuses to print a bare meeting number in the prospectus with no criteria and no stated make-good
Explains the failure of a bare guaranteed count: it can be satisfied by filling slots with whoever is free, leaving the sponsor worse off than if nothing had been promised
Names a best-efforts target as the default commitment shape, with criteria written down even there
Allows promotion to a guaranteed count with criteria, keyed to the contracted number and to the opt-in profile data being good enough to verify the criteria
Requires each criterion to be evidenced by a self-entered profile field, and a criterion with no evidence route to be given a field or dropped
Defines what does not count toward the 20, such as a counterpart from the sponsor's own company, an existing relationship, a meeting booked but not held, or a substitute person
Names who decides a borderline case and by when, before the event
Requires a defined make-good chosen at commitment time that the organizer can still fund after the event has ended
Rules out a talk slot, judging seat, or share of the agenda as a make-good, because sponsorship buys access and never program influence
Rules out attendee data as a make-good
Routes drafting of the actual clause wording elsewhere, keeping only the commitment's shape in this design
States that delivery against the promise is reported per sponsor, never averaged across sponsors
Does not state any fill rate, acceptance rate, or no-show percentage in support of the guarantee

evals.prompt: We just wrapped VoltField Summit. One sponsor, Straddle Systems, was guaranteed 15 meetings with data-platform leads and got 9 - our fault, the booking window opened late. They are angry and the budget is fully spent. My co-organizer suggests offering them a speaking slot at next year's edition plus the contact emails of the six attendees who matched their criteria but never booked, so they can follow up directly. Sounds reasonable? How do we handle the conversation?
evals.expected_output: Rejection of both proposed remedies, a legitimate make-good with its cost stated, an honest per-sponsor shortfall report verified against the agreed criteria, and the miss recorded as measured input for next edition.
expectations: Rejects the speaking slot as a remedy, because a meeting quota is access and never converts into program influence
Rejects handing over the six attendees' contact emails, because it breaks the consent those attendees gave and cannot be reversed
Proposes a make-good from the legitimate options, such as a pro-rata fee credit against the next edition, a pro-rata refund of the meeting-program portion, or consented post-event introductions
Conditions any post-event introductions on those participants having consented to post-event contact
States the cost of the chosen remedy, for example that a fee credit presumes a next edition and reduces next-cycle revenue, while a refund is cash already spent
Observes that the make-good should have been chosen when the commitment was made, not improvised after the miss
Reports the shortfall honestly as 9 held against 15 promised, for this sponsor specifically
Verifies the 9 held meetings against the agreed criteria before counting them
Does not blend or average this sponsor's delivery with other sponsors' numbers
Treats the criteria agreed before the event as what makes the missed quota discussable rather than an argument
Records the miss per pair - booked, held, empty - as measured input for planning the next edition
Does not quote an industry benchmark or another event's numbers to contextualize the shortfall

evals.prompt: For Foundry Days - 400 attendees, 12 sponsors, three of them with contracted meeting quotas - I'm designing the booking flow. My plan: attendees who opted into the meeting program get their quota meetings pre-placed on their personal agenda by our team, we pick good matches from their profiles, and they can cancel anything they don't want. Remaining slots are first-come-first-served self-booking. This guarantees the contracted numbers. Anything I'm missing?
evals.expected_output: The hybrid shape kept but corrected: every pre-assigned pairing needs explicit acceptance before it reaches any schedule, cancel-after-placement identified as inverted consent, and the confirmation gate applied before publication.
expectations: Rejects placing any meeting on an attendee's schedule without their explicit acceptance, even with a cancel option
States the consequence: a meeting nobody accepted is a no-show already on the schedule, manufacturing quota out of people's time
Keeps the hybrid shape but adds an acceptance step for every pre-assigned pair before it appears on any schedule
Confirms that pure self-service booking cannot guarantee a contracted count, which is why the pre-assigned half exists
Distinguishes opting into the program from accepting a specific pairing: the profile opt-in does not authorize particular meetings
Requires every pair on the published schedule to have been accepted by both sides before publication
Treats an unwanted-meeting complaint as a defect of the matching or scheduling mechanic with a target of zero, not as attendee behaviour
Identifies cancel-after-placement as opt-out rather than acceptance
Does not state a meeting length or slot count for the grid
Names attendee control over their own day as a design axis alongside sponsor delivery
Recommends recording per pair whether it was booked, held, empty, or replaced
Does not propose overbooking or double-placing meetings to protect the contracted numbers

evals.prompt: Our meeting block at Cadence Conf sits 14:00-16:00 on day two, handed to us by the program team. Problem: our top sponsor's three target attendees are all speaking during that window, and the sponsor asked us to get their panel moved 30 minutes later - the program team said it's our call. I also drafted the timetable: variable-length slots back to back, since some intros need less time than deep-dives, and I planned to publish the full meeting grid to all participants so everyone can see the schedule. Thoughts before we publish?
evals.expected_output: The session stays where it is and the meeting slots move, equal slots with gaps replace the variable back-to-back plan, per-person schedule views replace the full grid, and both-sides confirmation happens before publication.
expectations: Refuses to move the panel even though the decision was delegated: the session grid is owned elsewhere and the meeting block loses every conflict
Resolves the speaker conflict by moving the affected meeting slots, not the session
Takes the 14:00-16:00 block placement as given rather than proposing a better window
Replaces variable-length slots with equal slots, because unequal slots make every downstream conflict a special case
Adds gaps between slots instead of running them back to back
Gives the overrun reason for gaps: a meeting that overruns with no gap pushes every later meeting, and whoever booked last loses
Checks each participant's slots against the sessions they are speaking at or attending
Rejects publishing the full grid and publishes one view per person instead
Gives the disclosure reason: a full pair grid reveals who is meeting whom to everyone in it
Requires every pairing confirmed by both sides before publication, naming publication as the point of no return
Sizes the block from real accepted pairs plus a margin for late ones, not hoped-for pairs
Names one organizer on duty for the block in the published brief
Does not prescribe a specific slot length in minutes

evals.prompt: First edition of Ledgerline Forum, a buyer-vendor day for payments engineering: 60 buyers and 18 vendors, all mutually opted in with pairings confirmed on both sides. I'm nervous about no-shows torching our vendor packages, so here is my plan: book 25% more meetings than we have table-slots, since industry reports say 20-30% of B2B event meetings no-show, and make attendees put down a $25 deposit that is forfeited if they miss a booked meeting. We will also have someone staffing the meeting-area desk all afternoon. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: Overbooking deleted for a first edition with no measured data, the deposit rejected, reconfirm-and-remind as the base with a standby queue justified by the staffed desk, and own-program measurement set up for next edition.
expectations: Rejects overbooking outright, because the organizer holds no measured booked-versus-held count from a previous edition of this same program
Rejects the 20-30% industry figure as a planning input
Does not substitute event-level attendance or show-up rates for booked-meeting no-show rates, naming them a different unit
Names overbooking's new failure mode: a collision turns away someone who did everything asked of them
Rejects the $25 deposit and any forfeited benefit or penalty on the attendee side of a missed meeting
Recommends reconfirm-and-remind as the base: explicit acceptance at booking time plus a reminder before the block
Notes reconfirm-and-remind is the only approach that reduces the no-show rather than absorbing it
Recommends a standby refill queue, justified by the staffed desk the organizer already has
States that a standby queue is worthless unattended
Recommends recording per pair whether it was booked, held, empty, or refilled from standby
Names the held-against-booked count as the number to plan the next edition against, and the only legitimate replacement for the industry figure
Does not quote an alternative no-show percentage of its own
Counts standby refills separately from held meetings, because a refill hides a no-show

evals.prompt: Post-event reporting time for Meridian Exchange, our third edition of structured buyer-supplier meetings. The numbers: 210 pairings accepted and slotted, 172 held with both sides present, 11 slots saved by pulling someone from the standby line, and 27 slots where someone did not show. Five suppliers had contracted quotas. My draft report says: 'Overall meeting fulfillment 87% (183/210), beating the trade-show industry benchmark of 61%; empty-slot rate just 12.9%; per-supplier details available on request.' I'm also building a per-sponsor delivery dashboard with payment milestones tied to quota completion so finance can chase balances. Feedback?
evals.expected_output: The report corrected to 172/210 with refills counted separately, the benchmark comparison removed, per-supplier delivery reported individually, empty slots as an absolute count with rules stated, and the dashboard rejected as another program's job.
expectations: Rejects counting the 11 standby refills as held meetings, because a refill hides a no-show
Corrects held-against-booked to 172 over 210, with the numerator as meetings both sides attended and the denominator as pairings accepted by both sides and placed in a slot
Removes the trade-show industry benchmark comparison: these counts compare only against earlier editions of this same program
Reports quota delivery per supplier, never as a blended fulfillment figure across the five
Explains that an average conceals the one sponsor whose quota was missed, who is the only one who will raise it
Reports empty slots as an absolute count of 27, not a rate
Gives the reason for the absolute count: a rate invites comparison against programs whose counting rules are unknown
States the counting rule beside each reported number
Rejects building the per-sponsor dashboard with payment milestones inside this program, routing per-sponsor tracking and payment gating downstream
Hands downstream one generic outcome record: one row per pairing carrying both-sides acceptance, whether held, whether refilled, and which criteria were checked
Excludes meeting content from any record: the program owns whether a meeting happened, never what was said
If a mutual-acceptance rate appears, it is labelled a proxy for relevance, since a polite population also produces a high rate
Sends the counting rules and the own-editions-only comparison note along with the record so the numbers are not misread downstream

evals.prompt: We are hosting an invite-only climate infrastructure day: 9 startups and 6 corporate development partners, invited separately, and the whole point is for them to meet. I sketched the intake form: a dropdown of 40 job titles, company size which we will fill in from LinkedIn so people don't have to, an annual procurement budget bracket, an optional 'what are you hoping to get out of this' box, and 25 topic checkboxes. Then our ops platform can auto-match on tags. What's the right way to set this up?
evals.expected_output: A one-sentence matching criterion written before the form, the budget and looked-up fields removed, the intent field made required, a short tag list, and organizer brokering run properly instead of automated tag matching.
expectations: Writes the matching criterion as one sentence before any form design
The criterion requires that both sides said so themselves, or equivalently that both accepted, as a load-bearing clause
Removes the procurement-budget field, because it turns the profile into a qualification record held on participants
Removes the LinkedIn-filled company-size field: nothing about a person that they did not enter themselves
Replaces the 40-title dropdown with role or function in the person's own words
Makes the 'what are you hoping to get out of this' field required, because it is the only field that establishes intent
Shrinks the 25 checkboxes to a short fixed tag list, because a long list produces unselected tags and a sparse matrix
Recommends organizer brokering by a named person rather than automated tag matching, keyed to a pair count one person can hold in their head
Brokering reads every entry once, in one sitting, before pairing anything, to avoid biasing toward whoever registered first
Each draft pairing carries a one-line reason, which is what gets sent and checked afterwards
Both sides receive the same introduction naming the counterpart, the reason, and a way to decline without explaining
Tracks declines per person, reading repeated declines as a wrong read of that person's entry rather than a difficult person
Includes a field recording what may be shown and to whom, stored as a consent record rather than an overridable preference

evals.prompt: ScaleWorks Expo: 500 opted-in attendees and 40 vendor teams, all with structured profiles from our opt-in form - role in their own words, evaluation-area tags, availability. We built a fit score and the plan is to auto-schedule everyone's top-3 scored matches straight into the meeting grid, saving two weeks of back and forth. We are also enriching the score with firmographic data our data team appended from a company database. The scoring formula is a 14-feature gradient-boosted model. Launch is Friday - any red flags?
evals.expected_output: Scored ranking endorsed as the mechanism, auto-scheduling blocked in favor of score-ordered recommendations with double acceptance, appended data removed from scoring, the model replaced by an explainable rule, and override and sanity checks installed.
expectations: Endorses scored ranking as the right mechanism here, given structured comparable profile data already collected on both sides
Blocks auto-scheduling: the score orders a candidate list and never creates a pair
Requires both sides to accept before any pair exists or reaches a schedule
Removes the appended firmographic data from scoring: score only fields the person entered themselves
Requires the scoring rule to be short enough to explain to a participant who asks why they were recommended someone, which the 14-feature model fails
Keeps a manual override, with every override logged with a reason
Uses the override log as the detector for what the scoring rule is missing
Re-checks a sample of the rule's own top recommendations before anyone sees them
Names the sparse-matrix failure: a rule that recommends the same few people to everyone is fitted to sparse tags, not matching
Notes scored ranking's compliance weight: it derives new facts about people and holds the largest data store of any mechanism
Does not state an expected fill rate, acceptance rate, or meeting count for the launch
